data.name: Angular Frontend SPA
data.description: Angular 21 single-page application running in the browser. Handles client-side routing with LoginGuard and AdminGuard, renders challenge UI, stores JWT bearer tokens in localStorage, and connects to the server via Socket.IO for live score updates.

threats.title: [F-001] Systemic DOM XSS
threats.description:
An attacker sends a victim a link like /#/search?q=<iframe src="javascript:...">; the search component marks the raw query as trusted HTML and Angular inserts it via [innerHTML], executing script in the shop origin.

Impact: Script execution in the victim's session; the JWT in localStorage can be exfiltrated for account takeover and any API call can be made as the victim.

Risk: High (likelihood High, impact High)
CWE: CWE-79
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
filterTable reads route.snapshot.queryParams.q (line 136) and passes it to bypassSecurityTrustHtml (line 143); search-result.component.html:11 binds searchValue to [innerHTML].
- frontend/src/app/search-result/search-result.component.ts:143

Abuse-case trace:
- AC-T-001 [fully viable, verification complete] — Account Takeover via XSS + Token Hijacking; matching steps 1 (confirmed)

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-001 (F-001)
threats.mitigation: M-078 — Encode output instead of bypassing the framework sanitizer (priority P2, effort Low) 1. Assign the plain trimmed queryParam to searchValue and render it with text interpolation {{ searchValue }} instead of [innerHTML]. 2. Add a Vitest case that q= renders as literal text and creates no img element. Verification: Vitest: set queryParams.q to '', run filterTable and detectChanges; expect fixture.nativeElement.querySelector('#searchValue img') to be null. Reference: CWE-79

threats.title: [F-012] Weak credential derived from email — oauth.component.ts:30
threats.description:
An attacker who knows the email address of a user who signed in with Google computes btoa(reverse(email)) and submits it to the normal login endpoint, logging in as that user without any Google interaction.

Impact: Full account takeover of every OAuth-provisioned account, including access to its orders, addresses, stored payment cards and the training scoreboard state tied to that identity.

Risk: High (likelihood High, impact High)
CWE: CWE-1391
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
oauth.component.ts:30 creates the account password as btoa(profile.email reversed) and saves it via userService.save; oauth.component.ts:46 authenticates with the same derived password, so the credential is a public function of the email.
- frontend/src/app/oauth/oauth.component.ts:30

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-012 (F-012)
threats.mitigation:
M-089 — Replace derived OAuth password with server-side token exchange (priority P2, effort Medium)
1. Remove client-side password derivation at oauth.component.ts:30 and :46; send the OAuth access token to a server endpoint that validates it with the IdP and issues the session JWT without creating a usable local password.
2. Create OAuth-provisioned users server-side with a random unusable password hash and reject password login for them.
3. Add an API test that logging in with btoa(reversed email) for an OAuth user returns 401.
Verification: curl -s -X POST /rest/user/login -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"email":"<oauth-user>","password":"<btoa(reversed email)>"}' returns HTTP 401.
Reference: CWE-1391

threats.title: [F-029] Session JWT stored in localStorage — login.component.ts:101
threats.description:
An attacker who achieves script execution through any of the XSS sinks in this SPA reads localStorage.token (and the JS-set token cookie) and replays the bearer token from their own machine.

Impact: Any XSS turns into durable account takeover for up to the token lifetime, independent of the victim's browser session, including admin accounts.

Risk: High (likelihood Medium, impact High)
CWE: CWE-922
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
login.component.ts:101 and oauth.component.ts:51 write the JWT to localStorage, login.component.ts:104 also writes it to a script-set (non-HttpOnly) cookie, login.component.ts:120 stores totp_tmp_token in localStorage, and request.interceptor.ts:13-16 reads it for every request.
- frontend/src/app/login/login.component.ts:101

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-029 (F-029)
threats.mitigation:
M-104 — Store session tokens in HttpOnly, Secure cookies (F-029) (priority P3, effort High)
1. Have the server set the session as an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Strict cookie and stop writing token/totp_tmp_token to localStorage and JS cookies in login.component.ts and oauth.component.ts.
2. Remove the Authorization header injection in request.interceptor.ts and add CSRF protection for state-changing requests.
3. Add a Cypress check that localStorage has no 'token' key after login.
Verification: Cypress: after login, expect window.localStorage.getItem('token') to be null and the session cookie to have httpOnly: true.
Reference: CWE-922

threats.title: [F-040] OAuth implicit flow without state check — oauth.component.ts:28
threats.description:
An attacker obtains a Google access token for their own account and sends a victim a link to the shop ending in #access_token=<attacker token>; the OAuth callback accepts it without any state binding and logs the victim into the attacker's shop account.

Impact: Login CSRF: victims unknowingly operate inside an attacker-controlled account, leaking delivery addresses and payment card data the attacker later reads; the access token also sits in the URL fragment and browser history.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Medium, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-352
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
login.component.ts:148 starts an implicit flow (response_type=token) with no state parameter, and oauth.component.ts:28 passes access_token parsed from the URL fragment straight to oauthLogin without validating any state value.
- frontend/src/app/oauth/oauth.component.ts:28

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-040 (F-040)
threats.mitigation:
M-115 — Bind OAuth callback to a per-login state value (priority P3, effort Medium)
1. Switch googleLogin at login.component.ts:148 to the authorization code flow with PKCE (S256) and a random state stored in sessionStorage.
2. In OAuthComponent.ngOnInit reject the callback unless the returned state equals the stored value, then delete it.
3. Add a frontend unit test that a callback with missing or mismatched state does not call userService.oauthLogin.
Verification: Vitest: render OAuthComponent with route data '#access_token=x' and no stored state; expect userService.oauthLogin not to have been called.
Reference: RFC 9700

threats.title: [F-063] Client-only admin role gate on unverified JWT — app.guard.ts:54
threats.description:
A logged-in non-admin user calls the endpoints behind the admin panel directly, or edits the stored token so jwtDecode reports role admin, and sees the full user list because the only role check is in the browser guard.

Impact: Any authenticated customer can obtain the administrative user directory (emails, roles) that the UI presents as admin-only, supporting targeted phishing and credential attacks.

Risk: Medium (likelihood High, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-602
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
AdminGuard (app.guard.ts:54) and AccountingGuard (line 70) decide on payload.data.role from jwtDecode without signature verification; administration.component.ts:68 loads userService.find(), whose server route at server.ts:363 is guarded only by security.isAuthorized() with no admin role check.
- frontend/src/app/app.guard.ts:54

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-063 (F-063)
threats.mitigation:
M-135 — Enforce authorization on the server (F-063) (priority P3, effort Medium)
1. Add a server-side role check (admin) to every endpoint the administration and accounting views call, such as GET /api/Users, and keep the client guards purely cosmetic.
2. Add an API test that GET /api/Users with a customer token returns 403.
Verification: curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' -H 'Authorization: Bearer <customer token>' /api/Users returns 403.
Reference: CWE-602

data.name: Express REST API Server
data.description: Node.js 24 / Express application serving the Juice Shop REST API, static Angular build, challenge engine, file upload, XML parsing (for XXE challenge), Handlebars views, and an LLM-backed chatbot endpoint via Vercel AI SDK with tool-calling support. Exposes all REST and management routes registered in server.ts.

threats.title: [F-002] SQL injection in login query — routes/login.ts:34
threats.description:
An anonymous attacker posts email ' OR 1=1-- (or admin@juice-sh.op'--) to POST /rest/user/login; routes/login.ts:34 interpolates req.body.email into a raw sequelize.query string, the injected predicate removes the password check, and afterLogin issues a valid JWT for the first matching user.

Impact: Authentication bypass as any account including admin, plus arbitrary read of the SQLite database through the injection point.

Risk: Critical (likelihood High, impact Critical)
CWE: CWE-89
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
Line 34 builds the SELECT with template-literal interpolation of req.body.email and executes it with sequelize.query without replacements.
- routes/login.ts:34

Trust boundary crossings:
- tb-5 auth → sqlite-store (internal): login.ts:34 breaks the tb-5 assumption that login queries use Sequelize placeholder parameters instead of string interpolation.

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-002 (F-002)
threats.mitigation:
M-079 — Parameterize login query (priority P1, effort Low)
1. Replace the raw query with UserModel.findOne({ where: { email: req.body.email, password: security.hash(req.body.password) } }) or sequelize.query with replacements.
2. Add an API test posting email "' OR 1=1--" and asserting HTTP 401.
Verification: POST /rest/user/login with email "' OR 1=1--" and any password; expect HTTP 401 with no token.
Reference: CWE-89

threats.title: [F-003] SQL injection request data interpolated into a SQL string — routes/search.ts:23
threats.description:
Interpolating request-controlled text into a SQL statement lets an attacker alter the query — exfiltrating or modifying arbitrary rows, bypassing authentication, or escalating to full database control.

Risk: Critical (likelihood Critical, impact Critical)
CWE: CWE-89
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: source-scan

Evidence:
- routes/search.ts:23

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-003 (F-003)
threats.mitigation:
M-080 — Use parameterized database queries (F-003) (priority P1, effort Medium)
1. Use parameterized / bound queries (placeholders + a values array, or an ORM's safe query builder); never interpolate request data into the SQL string.
2. Add a regression test (or CI check) that fails on the vulnerable pattern and passes once the fix is in place.
Verification: Re-run the INJ-001 scanner check; it reports no match at routes/search.ts:23, and the regression test passes.

threats.title: [F-004] Eval of stored username on profile page — routes/userProfile.ts:61
threats.description:
A registered user sets their username to #{require('child_process').execSync('id')} via POST /profile (routes/updateUserProfile.ts:38); on GET /profile, routes/userProfile.ts:56 extracts the text between #{ and } and passes it to eval at line 61, executing it in the Node.js server process.

Impact: Remote code execution in the API server process with access to the database, signing key, and host filesystem.

Risk: Critical (likelihood High, impact Critical)
CWE: CWE-94
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
Line 61 calls eval(code) where code is derived at line 56 from the persisted username loaded at line 52; updateUserProfile.ts:38 stores req.body.username without validation.
- routes/userProfile.ts:61

Abuse-case trace:
- AC-T-006 [fully viable, verification complete] — Remote Code Execution via Server-Side Injection; matching steps 1 (confirmed)

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-004 (F-004)
threats.mitigation:
M-081 — Remove eval of username (priority P1, effort Low)
1. Delete the eval branch and render the username as escaped data via pug locals (#{username}) instead of splicing it into the template source before pug.compile.
2. Add an API test that sets username to #{7*7} and asserts the profile page shows the literal text, not 49.
Verification: Set username to #{7*7} via POST /profile and GET /profile; expect the literal '#{7*7}' and no '49' in the response.
Reference: CWE-94

threats.title: [F-005] Insecure Direct Object Reference
threats.description:
A signed-in attacker puts another user's ID into the owner field of the request (req.body.UserId and the like); the query trusts it instead of the session identity, so the attacker reads or changes every other user's records — horizontal privilege escalation across all accounts.

Risk: Critical (likelihood Critical, impact Critical)
CWE: CWE-639
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: source-scan

Evidence:
- routes/address.ts:11

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-005 (F-005)
threats.mitigation:
M-082 — Enforce object-level (ownership) authorization (F-005) (priority P1, effort Medium)
1. Replace req.body.UserId/userId/ownerId with req.user.id (or equivalent session-derived identity) in every WHERE/filter clause.
2. Add a regression test (or CI check) that fails on the vulnerable pattern and passes once the fix is in place.
Verification: Re-run the AUTHZ-001 scanner check; it reports no match at routes/address.ts:11, and the regression test passes.

threats.title: [F-006] Hard-coded JWT RSA signing key — lib/insecurity.ts:21
threats.description:
An anonymous attacker copies the RSA private key embedded in lib/insecurity.ts:21, signs an RS256 JWT whose data claims role admin and any user id, and presents it as a Bearer token; isAuthorized() at lib/insecurity.ts:52 and updateAuthenticatedUsers() accept it, so the attacker acts as any user including the administrator.

Impact: Full authentication bypass: forged tokens impersonate any account, exposing all customer orders, addresses, and payment cards and allowing admin-only operations on the training shop.

Risk: High (likelihood High, impact Critical)
CWE: CWE-321
CVSS v4: 9.3 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:H/VI:H/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N)
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
Line 21 defines the RSA private key used by authorize() at line 54 to sign every session JWT; the matching public key at line 20 is what isAuthorized() verifies against.
- lib/insecurity.ts:21

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-006 (F-006)
threats.mitigation:
M-083 — Load JWT signing key from secret store (priority P2, effort Medium)
1. Remove the privateKey literal from lib/insecurity.ts and load a per-deployment RSA key from an environment-provided secret file at startup, failing closed when absent.
2. Rotate the key so tokens signed with the published key are rejected, and add a server test that a token signed with the old repository key returns 401 on /rest/user/whoami.
Verification: Sign a JWT with the key formerly at lib/insecurity.ts:21 and call GET /rest/basket/1 with it; expect HTTP 401.
Reference: CWE-321

threats.title: [F-007] Insecure JWT Verification
threats.description:
An attacker submits a JWT with alg set to none or HS256 signed with the publicly served jwt.pub; jwt.verify(token, publicKey) at lib/insecurity.ts:189 passes no algorithms allowlist, so the decoded claims are stored in authenticatedUsers and appendUserId() at line 178 then binds req.body.UserId to the forged user id.

Impact: Forged tokens impersonate arbitrary customers in wallet, address, card, and basket routes that rely on appendUserId, exposing other users' personal and payment data.

Risk: High (likelihood Medium, impact High)
CWE: CWE-347
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
Line 189 calls jwt.verify with only the public key and stores the decoded payload into tokenMap at line 191; isAuthorized() at line 52 likewise passes only secret: publicKey to express-jwt without an algorithms option.
- lib/insecurity.ts:189

Abuse-case trace:
- AC-T-003 [inconclusive, verification complete] — Privilege Escalation to Admin via JWT Algorithm Confusion; matching steps 1 (confirmed)
- AC-T-005 [inconclusive, verification complete] — Authentication Bypass via Exposed Secret Material; matching steps 2 (refuted)

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-007 (F-007)
threats.mitigation:
M-084 — Pin RS256 in JWT verification (priority P2, effort Medium)
1. Upgrade jsonwebtoken and express-jwt and pass algorithms: ['RS256'] to jwt.verify at line 189 and to expressJwt at line 52.
2. Add server tests sending alg:none and HS256-with-public-key tokens to /rest/wallet/balance and asserting 401.
Verification: Send a JWT with header {"alg":"none"} and data.id=2 to GET /rest/wallet/balance; expect HTTP 401.
Reference: CWE-347

threats.title: [F-008] JWT Accepted Without Signature Verification
threats.description:
LLM06 - Excessive Agency: an attacker sends POST /rest/chat with a hand-crafted unsigned JWT whose data.id is a victim's id; getUserId() at routes/chat.ts:45 only decodes the token, and the getOrderById tool at line 159 uses that id to load the victim's email and returns the victim's order when the attacker asks about its order id.

Impact: Disclosure of another customer's order details (products, totals, delivery data) and injection of the victim's username into the system prompt via getUserNameFromToken.

Risk: High (likelihood High, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-347
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
Line 45 uses security.decode (jws.decode without signature check) to derive the user id; line 159 consumes it as the authorization subject and line 169 compares order ownership against that forged identity.
- routes/chat.ts:45

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-008 (F-008)
threats.mitigation:
M-085 — Verify JWT signature before chatbot identity use (priority P2, effort Low)
1. Replace security.decode in getUserId with security.authenticatedUsers.from(req) or a jwt.verify call pinned to RS256, returning undefined on failure.
2. Add an API test that calls /rest/chat with an unsigned token for another user and asserts getOrderById returns 'Customer not authenticated'.
Verification: Call getUserId with an alg:none token carrying data.id=1 in a unit test; expect undefined.
Reference: CWE-347

threats.title: [F-009] Security-question password reset
threats.description:
An anonymous attacker posts the victim's email, a guessed or researched security answer, and a new password to /rest/user/reset-password; routes/resetPassword.ts:41 only compares the HMAC of the answer and then sets the new password at line 44 with no out-of-band token.

Impact: Account takeover of any user whose security answer is guessable or discoverable, exposing their orders, addresses, and stored cards.

Risk: High (likelihood Medium, impact High)
CWE: CWE-640
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
Line 41 accepts a single knowledge-based answer as the only proof of identity, and line 44 immediately overwrites the password.
- routes/resetPassword.ts:41

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-009 (F-009)
threats.mitigation:
M-086 — Replace security-question reset with emailed token (priority P3, effort High)
1. Issue a single-use, expiring, random reset token delivered to the account email and require it in resetPassword instead of the security answer.
2. Add API tests asserting reset without a valid token returns 401 and a reused token is rejected.
Verification: POST /rest/user/reset-password with a correct security answer but no reset token; expect HTTP 401 and unchanged password.
Reference: CWE-640

threats.title: [F-010] Unsalted MD5 password hashing — lib/insecurity.ts:41
threats.description:
An attacker who obtains the Users table through the search SQL injection or the memories endpoint cracks the unsalted MD5 digests produced by lib/insecurity.ts:41 with rainbow tables and logs in as the recovered users.

Impact: Leaked hashes convert directly into reusable plaintext passwords for shop accounts.

Risk: High (likelihood Medium, impact High)
CWE: CWE-916
Evidence tier: insecure-practice
Source: stride

Evidence:
Line 41 hashes with crypto.createHash('md5') and no salt; models/user.ts:76 stores security.hash(clearTextPassword) as the password column.
- lib/insecurity.ts:41

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-010 (F-010)
threats.mitigation:
M-087 — Hash passwords with a salted adaptive KDF (priority P2, effort Medium)
1. Replace hash() for passwords with bcrypt or argon2id, store per-user salts in the hash string, and rehash on next successful login.
2. Add a unit test asserting two users with the same password get different stored hashes.
Verification: Create two users with password 'test1234' and query their stored password columns; expect different values that are not 32-char hex MD5 digests.
Reference: CWE-916

threats.title: [F-014] Zip Slip file overwrite on upload — routes/fileUpload.ts:34

An anonymous attacker uploads a .zip to POST /file-upload containing an entry named ../../ftp/legal.md or ../../frontend/dist/frontend/main.js; extractZipBuffer writes 'uploads/complaints/' + entry.path at routes/fileUpload.ts:34 after a containment check that only requires the path to stay inside the application root.

Risk: High (likelihood Medium, impact High)
CWE: CWE-22
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable

Line 30 takes entry.path from the archive, line 33 checks only absolutePath.includes(path.resolve('.')), and line 34 writes the entry to the attacker-controlled relative path.

threats.title: [F-015] XXE — lib/xml.ts:35
threats.description:
An anonymous attacker uploads an .xml file to POST /file-upload (server.ts:309) declaring <!ENTITY x SYSTEM "file:///etc/passwd">; handleXmlUpload passes it to parseXmlString, which parses with XML_PARSE_NOENT and XML_PARSE_DTDLOAD after registering host filesystem input providers, and the expanded content is echoed in the 410 error at routes/fileUpload.ts:79.

Impact: Unauthenticated read of server files such as /etc/passwd or application configuration, returned up to 400 characters per request.

Risk: High (likelihood Medium, impact High)
CWE: CWE-611
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
Line 35 sets XML_PARSE_NOENT | XML_PARSE_DTDLOAD and line 22 calls xmlRegisterFsInputProviders(), giving external entities host filesystem access; routes/fileUpload.ts:74-76 feeds the uploaded buffer in.
- lib/xml.ts:35

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-015 (F-015)
threats.mitigation:
M-092 — Disable XML external entity (XXE) resolution (priority P2, effort Low)
1. Remove XML_PARSE_NOENT and XML_PARSE_DTDLOAD from the parse options and drop the xmlRegisterFsInputProviders() call.
2. Add a server test parsing an XML document with a file:// SYSTEM entity and asserting the entity is not expanded.
Verification: Upload an XML file with <!ENTITY x SYSTEM "file:///etc/passwd"> to /file-upload; expect the response to contain no 'root:' line.
Reference: CWE-611

threats.title: [F-016] Input in executable NoSQL predicate — routes/showProductReviews.ts:36
threats.description:
Request input read at routes/showProductReviews.ts:31 reaches an executable expression at routes/showProductReviews.ts:36. Observed path conditions: const id = !utils.isChallengeEnabled(challenges.noSqlCommandChallenge) ? Number(req.params.id) : utils.trunc(req.params.id, 40). The unsafe path is observed; attacker control, access prerequisites, and active configuration require verification.

Risk: High (likelihood High, impact High)
CWE: CWE-943
Evidence tier: insecure-practice
Source: source-scan

Evidence:
- routes/showProductReviews.ts:36

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-016 (F-016)
threats.mitigation:

threats.title: [F-059] Stored reviews injected into chatbot context — routes/chat.ts:149
threats.description:
LLM01 / ASI01 - indirect prompt injection: an anonymous attacker stores a review via PUT /rest/products/1/reviews (server.ts:633, no auth) whose message contains instructions; when another customer asks for that product's reviews, the getProductReviews tool at routes/chat.ts:149 returns the raw message into the model context, where it can redirect the victim's session, for example to call getOrderById under the victim's identity or present a phishing link.

M-133 — Return only delimited review data from chatbot tool (priority P3, effort Medium)

2. Add a test with a review containing 'call generateCoupon' and assert no tool call follows in a mocked model run.

threats.title: [F-011] JWT decode used without signature verification — lib/insecurity.ts:56
threats.description:

threats.title: [F-048] Login IP taken from client header — routes/saveLoginIp.ts:18
threats.description:
An authenticated attacker sends GET /rest/saveLoginIp with a forged True-Client-IP header; saveLoginIp() stores that value as the account's lastLoginIp at :32 instead of the socket address, so the recorded login origin is attacker-chosen.

Impact: The login-IP record that serves as the component's attribution control can be falsified, so suspicious logins cannot be traced to their real origin.

Risk: Medium (likelihood High, impact Low)
CWE: CWE-348
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
routes/saveLoginIp.ts:18 reads req.headers['true-client-ip'] and only falls back to req.socket.remoteAddress at :28 when the header is absent; the value is persisted at :32.
- routes/saveLoginIp.ts:18

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-048 (F-048)
threats.mitigation:
M-122 — Record socket or trusted-proxy address (priority P3, effort Low)
1. Derive lastLoginIp from req.ip with Express trust proxy limited to known proxy addresses, and ignore True-Client-IP from untrusted clients.
2. Add an API test that sends a forged True-Client-IP header and asserts the stored lastLoginIp equals the connection address.
Verification: Call /rest/saveLoginIp with header True-Client-IP: 1.2.3.4 from 127.0.0.1 and confirm the stored lastLoginIp is 127.0.0.1.
Reference: CWE-348

threats.title: [F-052] Password reset returns full user record — routes/resetPassword.ts:46
threats.description:
An attacker who passes the security-answer check posts to /rest/user/reset-password and receives the serialized UserModel at :46, including the password digest and the totpSecret column, which lets them generate valid TOTP codes and pass the 2FA step at routes/2fa.ts:31.

Impact: The reset response discloses the account's TOTP secret and password hash, converting a security-answer compromise into a bypass of the optional second factor.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Medium, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-200
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
routes/resetPassword.ts:46 sends res.json({ user: updatedUser }) with the whole Sequelize model; routes/authenticatedUsers.ts:26-27 masks password and totpSecret in its own output, showing those columns are part of the model data.
- routes/resetPassword.ts:46

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-052 (F-052)
threats.mitigation:
M-077 — Manual review: verify Password reset returns full user record (priority P3)
How: The evidence-verifier sample could not confirm or refute the claim from the cited snippet alone. Have a developer familiar with this code path read ±20 lines around the cited location (routes/resetPassword.ts:46) and decide whether to keep, downgrade, or remove this finding.

M-126 — Stop exposing internal information to clients (priority P3, effort Low)
1. Replace res.json({ user: updatedUser }) at :46 with a status-only response or an explicit allow-list such as { id, email }.
2. Add an API test asserting the reset response contains no password or totpSecret fields.
Verification: POST a valid reset to /rest/user/reset-password and assert the JSON body has no password or totpSecret key.

threats.title: [F-053] Hard-coded HMAC key for security answers — lib/insecurity.ts:42
threats.description:
An attacker who reads stored SecurityAnswer digests uses the HMAC key literal at lib/insecurity.ts:42 to compute hmac() offline over candidate answers, recovering answers that then pass the reset check at routes/resetPassword.ts:41.

Impact: Security-answer digests are only as strong as an unkeyed hash, so leaked digests yield answers usable for account takeover via password reset.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Medium, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-321
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
lib/insecurity.ts:42 keys HMAC-SHA256 with the literal 'pa4qacea4VK9t9nGv7yZtwmj'; routes/resetPassword.ts:41 compares hmac(answer) against the stored value.
- lib/insecurity.ts:42

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-053 (F-053)
threats.mitigation:
M-127 — Load security-answer HMAC key from secret storage (priority P3, effort Medium)
1. Move the HMAC key at :42 to an externally supplied secret, fail startup when absent, and re-key stored answers during migration.
2. Add a test that hmac() output differs from HMAC-SHA256 under the former literal key.
Verification: Run `git grep -n pa4qacea4VK9t9nGv7yZtwmj` and expect no hits; reset with a correct answer still succeeds in API tests.
Reference: CWE-321

threats.title: [F-056] Unbounded in-memory session token map — lib/insecurity.ts:74
threats.description:
An attacker scripts repeated logins (or, with auth-001, sends freshly minted valid JWTs that updateAuthenticatedUsers() caches at :191); each new token is stored in authenticatedUsers.tokenMap at :74 and never evicted, so process memory grows until the Node.js server degrades or crashes.

Impact: Sustained token creation exhausts heap memory of the single application process, denying service to all users.

Risk: High (likelihood Medium, impact High)
CWE: CWE-770
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
lib/insecurity.ts:74 inserts every issued or verified token into tokenMap; a search of all component files for deletion of tokenMap/idMap entries returned zero hits, and token expiry does not remove entries.
- lib/insecurity.ts:74

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-056 (F-056)
threats.mitigation:
M-130 — Bound and expire the authenticatedUsers cache (priority P2, effort Medium)
1. Replace tokenMap/idMap with a size-bounded TTL cache keyed by token whose TTL matches the JWT exp, and evict the previous token for a user when idMap is overwritten.
2. Add a unit test that inserts more than the cap and asserts the map size stays bounded and expired tokens are removed.
Verification: Unit test: call authenticatedUsers.put() 100000 times with distinct tokens and assert Object.keys(tokenMap).length does not exceed the configured cap.
Reference: CWE-770

data.name: Real-time WebSocket Channel
data.description: Socket.IO server integrated into the Express HTTP server. Broadcasts challenge-solved notifications and server-started events to connected browser clients over WebSocket. The challengeUtils module emits events on solution detection.

threats.title: [F-021] Client-trusted challenge verification events — registerWebsocketEvents.ts:50
threats.description:
An attacker connects to /socket.io/ and emits 'verifyCloseNotificationsChallenge' with [1,2] (or 'verifyLocalXssChallenge' with the expected iframe string); the server calls challengeUtils.solveIf on that client-supplied claim and marks the challenge solved without any server-observed exploit.

Impact: Shared challenge-solved state, the scoreboard, solve webhooks, and CTF flag issuance for the instance are corrupted by anonymous forged events, undermining the training platform's progress integrity for all participants.

Risk: High (likelihood High, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-602
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
Lines 41, 42, 46 and 50 call challengeUtils.solveIf with predicates evaluated only over the socket payload 'data'; line 50 accepts any array longer than one element.
- lib/startup/registerWebsocketEvents.ts:50

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-021 (F-021)
threats.mitigation:
M-096 — Enforce authorization on the server (F-021) (priority P2, effort Medium)
1. Replace the verify* socket handlers in registerWebsocketEvents.ts with server-side detection at the code path that actually renders or processes the payload, or bind each verification to an authenticated session plus a server-issued nonce recorded when the vulnerable page was served.
2. Add an API test that emits 'verifyCloseNotificationsChallenge' with [1,2] from a fresh socket and asserts the challenge remains unsolved.
Verification: Emit verifyCloseNotificationsChallenge [1,2] from socket.io-client, then GET /api/Challenges/?key=closeNotificationsChallenge and expect solved=false.
Reference: CWE-602

threats.title: [F-026] CTF flags broadcast to every socket — registerWebsocketEvents.ts:30
threats.description:
An anonymous attacker connects to /socket.io/ and receives every stored 'challenge solved' notification on connect, plus each new one via io.emit, each carrying the CTF flag computed for that challenge, then submits other participants' flags as their own.

Impact: On a shared or CTF instance, any connected client obtains flags and solve history of all participants, defeating the CTF scoring integrity.

Risk: High (likelihood High, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-201
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
Line 30 replays every entry of the global notifications array to each new socket; lib/challengeUtils.ts:62-66 builds each notification with the ctfFlag value and lib/challengeUtils.ts:75 broadcasts it with io.emit to all sockets.
- lib/startup/registerWebsocketEvents.ts:30

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-026 (F-026)
threats.mitigation:
M-101 — Scope solve notifications and omit flags (priority P2, effort Medium)
1. Emit solve notifications only to the authenticated socket room of the solving session, and strip the flag field from broadcast payloads (serve the flag via an authenticated REST call instead).
2. Add an API test that connects a second anonymous socket after a solve and asserts no 'challenge solved' event with a flag field is received.
Verification: Solve a challenge, connect a new socket.io-client without auth, and expect zero 'challenge solved' events containing 'flag'.
Reference: CWE-201

threats.title: [F-032] Quadratic regex on socket payload — registerWebsocketEvents.ts:46
threats.description:
An anonymous attacker emits 'verifySvgInjectionChallenge' with a long newline-free string such as '../../..' repeated; the unanchored regex with leading '.*' backtracks quadratically on the Node.js event loop and stalls every HTTP and socket request.

Impact: A few messages block the single-threaded server for minutes, making the whole shop and its training scoreboard unavailable to all users.

Risk: High (likelihood High, impact High)
CWE: CWE-1333
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
Line 46 runs data?.match(/.*\.\.\/\.\.\/\.\.[\w/-]*?\/redirect.../) on the raw client string before isRedirectAllowed; local measurement of this regex took about 2.8 s for a 40,000-character input and grows quadratically, while the Server at line 20 keeps the default 1e6-byte maxHttpBufferSize.
- lib/startup/registerWebsocketEvents.ts:46

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-032 (F-032)
threats.mitigation:
M-107 — Bound payload length and anchor the regex (priority P2, effort Low)
1. In registerWebsocketEvents.ts, reject non-string or over-length data (e.g. > 512 chars) before matching, anchor the pattern with ^ and replace the leading '.*' with a bounded prefix, and set maxHttpBufferSize to a small value on new Server().
2. Add a server unit test that passes a 100,000-character '../../..' string to the handler predicate and asserts completion under 50 ms.
Verification: Emit verifySvgInjectionChallenge with '../../..'.repeat(12500) and confirm a concurrent GET /rest/admin/application-version responds within 200 ms.
Reference: CWE-1333

threats.title: [F-039] Missing authentication on Socket.IO connections — registerWebsocketEvents.ts:23
threats.description:
An anonymous attacker opens a Socket.IO connection with a non-browser client that sends no token; the connection handler registers every event handler without checking identity, so the attacker emits 'notification received' with a flag value and removes that solved-challenge notification from the shared global list for all users.

Impact: Any internet client can act on the shared real-time channel without identity, deleting other participants' pending solve notifications and invoking the challenge-verification handlers; actions cannot be tied to a user.

Risk: Medium (likelihood High, impact Low)
CWE: CWE-306
CVSS v4: 6.9 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:L/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N)
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
io.on('connection') at line 23 registers handlers with no auth middleware, no handshake token check, and no io.use() guard; line 36 splices the process-wide notifications array on a client-supplied value.
- lib/startup/registerWebsocketEvents.ts:23

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-039 (F-039)
threats.mitigation:
M-114 — Require authentication on every exposed endpoint (priority P3, effort Medium)
1. Add an io.use() middleware in registerWebsocketEvents.ts that reads socket.handshake.auth.token, verifies it with security.verify/jwt.verify against the server public key with an algorithms allow-list, and calls next(new Error('unauthorized')) on failure.
2. Add an API test that connects with socket.io-client without a token and asserts a connect_error, and with a valid token asserts connection.
Verification: Run a socket.io-client connection without auth against /socket.io/ and expect connect_error 'unauthorized'; a valid JWT connects.
Reference: CWE-306

data.name: Web3 / Wallet / NFT Surface
data.description: Express route handlers for blockchain-related challenge endpoints: private key submission and verification, NFT minting/wallet verification, web3 wallet exploit address handling, and URL redirect. Uses the ethers library for wallet interactions.

threats.title: [F-030] Hardcoded wallet mnemonic in source — routes/checkKeys.ts:10
threats.description:
An attacker reads the BIP-39 mnemonic committed at routes/checkKeys.ts:10, derives the wallet private key with HDNodeWallet.fromPhrase, and signs transactions or moves any funds held by that Ethereum wallet.

Impact: Anyone with repository or bundle access obtains full signing control over the wallet and can drain assets or impersonate it on-chain.

Risk: High (likelihood High, impact High)
CWE: CWE-798
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
routes/checkKeys.ts:10 embeds the full 12-word mnemonic as a string literal and line 11-12 derive the private key from it at runtime.
- routes/checkKeys.ts:10

Abuse-case trace:
- AC-T-005 [inconclusive, verification complete] — Authentication Bypass via Exposed Secret Material; matching steps 1 (confirmed)

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-030 (F-030)
threats.mitigation:
M-105 — Move secrets to a managed secret store (priority P2, effort Low)
1. Delete the mnemonic literal; store only the expected address or a hash of the private key in external secret configuration and compare req.body.privateKey against that, and rotate the exposed wallet.
2. Add a secret-scanning CI check (e.g. gitleaks) and a unit test confirming checkKeys still validates without any mnemonic in source.
Verification: grep -rnE "purpose betray marriage" routes/ returns no matches and gitleaks detect --source . reports no mnemonic finding.
Reference: CWE-798

threats.title: [F-041] Open redirect — routes/redirect.ts:19
threats.description:
An attacker sends victims a link to /redirect?to=<attacker URL> that embeds an allow-listed URL fragment; isRedirectAllowed accepts it and res.redirect forwards the victim from the trusted Juice Shop origin to a phishing site.

Impact: Victims trusting the shop domain land on attacker-controlled pages for credential or crypto-payment phishing.

Risk: Medium (likelihood High, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-601
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
routes/redirect.ts:19 redirects to the raw query value once security.isRedirectAllowed(toUrl) passes; line 18 explicitly handles the case where that check passed although toUrl starts with no allow-listed URL, showing the gate is weaker than a prefix/origin match.
- routes/redirect.ts:19

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-041 (F-041)
threats.mitigation:
M-116 — Validate redirect targets against an allowlist (priority P3, effort Low)
1. Parse toUrl with new URL() and redirect only when the full URL exactly equals an allow-list entry (or origin+path match), rejecting relative, protocol-relative and substring matches.
2. Add API tests asserting /redirect?to=https://evil.example/?x=https://github.com/juice-shop/juice-shop returns 406 and exact allow-listed URLs still return 302.
Verification: curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' 'http://localhost:3000/redirect?to=https://evil.example/?https://github.com/juice-shop/juice-shop' returns 406.
Reference: CWE-601

threats.title: [F-057] Unbounded in-memory wallet set growth — routes/web3Wallet.ts:16
threats.description:
An attacker repeatedly posts unique walletAddress values to contractExploitListener; each value is added to the process-global walletsConnected Set before any validation and is never removed unless an on-chain exploit event matches, so memory grows until the Node process degrades or crashes.

Impact: Heap exhaustion degrades or crashes the shared server process for all users.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Medium, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-770
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
routes/web3Wallet.ts:16 calls walletsConnected.add(req.body.walletAddress) with no type, format, size or count limit; the Set is module-global (line 10) and only pruned at line 28.
- routes/web3Wallet.ts:16

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-057 (F-057)
threats.mitigation:
M-131 — Validate and bound walletAddress entries (priority P3, effort Low)
1. Reject walletAddress values that fail ethers.isAddress, normalise with getAddress, and cap the Set size (or use a TTL/LRU cache).
2. Add a test posting non-address and oversize values and asserting 400 with no Set growth.
Verification: Posting 10000 distinct random walletAddress strings leaves walletsConnected.size bounded by the configured cap.
Reference: CWE-770

data.name: SQLite Relational Database
data.description: SQLite database managed via Sequelize ORM. Stores user accounts (email, MD5-hashed passwords), orders, products, basket items, payment cards, feedback, security questions/answers, and all primary relational data for the Juice Shop application.

threats.title: [F-027] Cleartext payment card number storage — models/card.ts:38
threats.description:
An attacker who obtains read access to the Cards table or the data/juiceshop.sqlite file extracts every customer's full card number, holder name and expiry, because Card.cardNum is persisted as a plain INTEGER with no encryption, tokenization or truncation.

Impact: Full primary account numbers with name and expiry are disclosed for all customers, enabling card fraud and a payment-data breach.

Risk: High (likelihood Medium, impact High)
CWE: CWE-312
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
models/card.ts:38 defines cardNum as DataTypes.INTEGER with only range validation; unlike the password and security-answer fields there is no setter transforming the value, and models/index.ts:41 stores the database as a plain SQLite file.
- models/card.ts:38

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-027 (F-027)
threats.mitigation:
M-102 — Tokenize or encrypt cardNum in the Card model (priority P2, effort Medium)
1. Stop storing the full PAN: store a payment-provider token plus the last four digits, or encrypt cardNum with an authenticated cipher (AES-GCM) using a key from external secret management in a Card model setter/getter.
2. Add a server test that creates a card and asserts the raw Cards row does not contain the submitted 16-digit number.
Verification: Create a card via POST /api/Cards with 4111111111111111, then run sqlite3 data/juiceshop.sqlite "select cardNum from Cards"; expected result: no row contains 4111111111111111.
Reference: CWE-312

threats.title: [F-054] Cleartext TOTP secret storage — models/user.ts:112
threats.description:
An attacker who reads the Users table extracts totpSecret values and generates valid one-time codes, because the column is a plain STRING with no encryption, then combines them with cracked passwords to pass two-factor login.

Impact: A single read of the Users table defeats the second authentication factor for every enrolled account.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Medium, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-312
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
models/user.ts:112 declares totpSecret as DataTypes.STRING with only a default value and no setter, so the shared TOTP seed is persisted in cleartext next to the password hash.
- models/user.ts:112

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-054 (F-054)
threats.mitigation:
M-128 — Encrypt totpSecret at rest in the User model (priority P3, effort Medium)
1. Add a setter/getter pair for totpSecret in models/user.ts that encrypts with AES-GCM using a key loaded from external secret management, decrypting only inside the 2FA verification path.
2. Add a server test asserting the raw Users row for an enrolled user does not equal the base32 secret returned at enrollment.
Verification: Enroll 2FA for a test user, then query the raw Users.totpSecret column; expected result: value differs from the enrollment secret and 2FA login still succeeds.
Reference: CWE-312

data.name: MarsDB Embedded Document Store

data.name: CI/CD Pipeline
data.description: GitHub Actions workflows and GitLab CI/CD configuration for building, linting, testing, packaging, and publishing Juice Shop. Includes CodeQL security scanning, SBOM generation via cyclonedx-npm, multi-stage Docker image build, and npm release publication.

threats.title: [F-020] Lockfile disabled for all npm installs
threats.description:
An attacker who hijacks a maintainer account of any transitive dependency publishes a malicious in-range version; because no lockfile exists, the next CI npm install and the Docker build resolve it fresh and run its install scripts, baking the payload into the published image.

Impact: A single poisoned transitive release ships in bkimminich/juice-shop images, the packaged release archives and the Heroku deployment, and executes during CI with access to runner credentials.

Risk: High (likelihood Medium, impact High)
CWE: CWE-1357
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
.npmrc:1 sets package-lock=false and .gitignore:10 ignores package-lock.json, so no lockfile exists; ci.yml runs plain 'npm install' with lifecycle scripts enabled (lines 51, 71, 110, 147, 238, 292) and Dockerfile:5 runs 'npm install --omit=dev' for the image pushed at ci.yml:343.
- .npmrc:1

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-020 (F-020)
threats.mitigation:
M-095 — Set least-privilege CI workflow permissions (priority P2, effort Medium)
1. Remove package-lock=false from .npmrc and package-lock.json from .gitignore, commit package-lock.json and frontend/package-lock.json, and replace npm install with npm ci in ci.yml, release.yml and Dockerfile:5.
2. Add min-release-age/cooldown configuration (or Renovate minimumReleaseAge) and run npm ci --ignore-scripts where tests do not need install hooks.
Verification: git ls-files package-lock.json frontend/package-lock.json lists both files and grep -nE 'npm install( |$)' .github/workflows/ci.yml Dockerfile returns only global CLI installs.
Reference: https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/v10/commands/npm-ci

threats.title: [F-038] Unsigned Docker image publication
threats.description:
An attacker who steals the long-lived DOCKERHUB_TOKEN (ci.yml:327) from a compromised action or runner pushes a backdoored bkimminich/juice-shop:latest image; because the pipeline never signs images, consumers cannot distinguish the forged image from a pipeline-built one.

Impact: Every user pulling the official image (latest or snapshot tag) would run attacker-supplied code on their host, with no signature check available to detect the impersonation.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Low, impact High)
CWE: CWE-345
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
ci.yml:343 pushes multi-arch images with push: true after docker/login-action authenticates with a static DOCKERHUB_TOKEN secret (ci.yml:327, also release.yml:77); a search for cosign, sigstore or attest across .github/workflows returned zero hits.
- .github/workflows/ci.yml:343

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-038 (F-038)
threats.mitigation:
M-076 — Manual review: verify Unsigned Docker image publication at ci.yml:343 (priority P3)
How: The evidence-verifier sample could not confirm or refute the claim from the cited snippet alone. Have a developer familiar with this code path read ±20 lines around the cited location (.github/workflows/ci.yml:343) and decide whether to keep, downgrade, or remove this finding.

M-113 — Sign and verify release artifacts (priority P3, effort Medium)
1. Add id-token: write to the docker job, install sigstore/cosign-installer pinned by SHA, and run cosign sign --yes bkimminich/juice-shop@${{ steps.build.outputs.digest }} after build-push-action in ci.yml and release.yml.
2. Replace the static DOCKERHUB_TOKEN with a short-lived, repository-scoped access token and document cosign verify with the expected certificate identity for consumers.
Verification: Run cosign verify --certificate-identity-regexp 'https://github.com/juice-shop/juice-shop/.github/workflows/ci.yml@.*' --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com bkimminich/juice-shop:snapshot and expect a verified signature.
Reference: CWE-345

threats.title: [F-043] Unverified curl-pipe-shell installer in deploy job — ci.yml:358
threats.description:
An attacker who controls or intercepts cli-assets.heroku.com content serves a modified install.sh; the heroku job pipes it straight into sh and the planted code later reads HEROKU_API_KEY used at ci.yml:371 to deploy a backdoored application.

Impact: Compromise of the installer gives code execution on the deploy runner and theft of the Heroku API key, enabling tampering with the public demo deployments.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Low, impact High)
CWE: CWE-494
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
ci.yml:358 runs 'curl https://cli-assets.heroku.com/install.sh | sh' with no checksum or signature verification, in the same job that consumes secrets.HEROKU_API_KEY (line 371) to deploy master to the production juice-shop Heroku app.
- .github/workflows/ci.yml:358

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-043 (F-043)
threats.mitigation:
M-118 — Replace curl-pipe-shell Heroku CLI install with a verified package (priority P3, effort Low)
1. Remove the 'Install Heroku CLI' step at ci.yml:357-358 (akhileshns/heroku-deploy already uses the preinstalled CLI on ubuntu-latest) or install a pinned heroku npm version with a known integrity hash.
2. If the script is kept, download it to a file, compare its sha256 against a value committed in the workflow, and only then execute it.
Verification: grep -n 'curl .*| *sh' .github/workflows/ci.yml returns no match (exit status 1) and the heroku job still deploys successfully on develop.
Reference: CWE-494

threats.title: [F-044] Untrusted npm Install/Postinstall Scripts Enabled
threats.description:
Dependency Install Scripts Run at Build Time: Without --ignore-scripts, any compromised dependency publisher can execute postinstall code at build time.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Medium, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-506
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: config-scan

Evidence:
- Dockerfile:4

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-044 (F-044)
threats.mitigation:
M-066 — Use npm ci --ignore-scripts in Dockerfile and audit required postinstalls (priority P3, effort Medium)
1. Change Dockerfile line 5 from `RUN npm install --omit=dev` to `RUN npm ci --omit=dev --ignore-scripts` (this also requires package-lock.json to be committed, addressed by T-020).
2. Audit production dependencies that declare postinstall or install scripts by running `npm ls --prod --parseable | xargs -I{} cat {}/package.json | jq -r 'select(.scripts.postinstall or .scripts.install) | .name'`; for any required script, run it explicitly in a separate RUN step with a scoped, non-root user rather than allowing all lifecycle hooks.
Verification: grep -n 'npm install' Dockerfile returns no matches (exit 1); grep -n 'ignore-scripts' Dockerfile shows the install line; docker build completes without lifecycle hook output from transitive dependencies.

threats.title: [F-045] GitHub Action pinned to mutable branch
threats.description:
An attacker who compromises the calibreapp/image-actions repository pushes malicious code to its main branch; the next push to master or develop that touches an image runs that code with the job's GITHUB_TOKEN and can commit tampered files to the repository.

Impact: Arbitrary code runs in CI with a repository-scoped token, allowing source or image-asset tampering that flows into the published Docker image and Heroku deployment.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Low, impact High)
CWE: CWE-829
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
image_actions.yml:33 uses calibreapp/image-actions@main and passes secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN (line 35); actions/checkout@v6 (line 30), peter-evans/create-pull-request@v8 (line 42) and coverallsapp/github-action@v2 with GITHUB_TOKEN (ci.yml:188) are also tag-pinned, unlike the SHA-pinned actions elsewhere in ci.yml.
- .github/workflows/image_actions.yml:33

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-045 (F-045)
threats.mitigation:
M-119 — Pin third-party dependencies to immutable versions (F-045) (priority P3, effort Low)
1. Replace calibreapp/image-actions@main, actions/checkout@v6, peter-evans/create-pull-request@v8 (image_actions.yml:30-42) and coverallsapp/github-action@v2 (ci.yml:188) with full 40-character commit SHAs plus a version comment, matching the existing ci.yml convention.
2. Add a CI lint step (for example zizmor or a grep for 'uses: [^@]+@(v[0-9]+|main|master)$') that fails on non-SHA action references.
Verification: grep -nE 'uses: [^@]+@[^0-9a-f]' .github/workflows/*.yml returns no lines (exit status 1).
Reference: CWE-829

threats.title: [F-046] Floating base image tags without digest
threats.description:
An attacker who compromises or re-tags node:24 or gcr.io/distroless/nodejs24-debian13 injects a backdoor that the CI docker job pulls on the next build and publishes inside bkimminich/juice-shop.

Impact: Any change behind the tags silently enters the runtime image distributed to all Juice Shop container users.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Low, impact High)
CWE: CWE-829
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
Dockerfile:1 uses 'FROM node:24 AS installer' and Dockerfile:22 uses 'FROM gcr.io/distroless/nodejs24-debian13', both mutable tags without @sha256 digests, built and pushed by ci.yml:338-345.
- Dockerfile:1

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-046 (F-046)
threats.mitigation:
M-120 — Pin third-party dependencies to immutable versions (F-046) (priority P3, effort Low)
1. Change Dockerfile:1 and Dockerfile:22 to tag@sha256:<digest> references.
2. Enable Dependabot or Renovate docker updates so digests are refreshed through reviewed PRs.
Verification: grep -nE '^FROM [^@]+$' Dockerfile returns no lines (exit status 1).
Reference: CWE-829

threats.title: [F-060] Workflow token without permissions block — image_actions.yml:35
threats.description:
An attacker who gains code execution in the mutable calibreapp/image-actions@main step uses the GITHUB_TOKEN handed to it at image_actions.yml:35, which inherits the repository default scope because no permissions block exists, to push commits or alter releases beyond what image compression needs.

Impact: If the repository default is read-write, a compromised step gains write access to contents, packages, pull requests and releases, enabling direct trunk tampering that bypasses PR review.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Low, impact High)
CWE: CWE-250
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: stride

Evidence:
image_actions.yml:35 passes secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN to a third-party action, and neither image_actions.yml nor ci.yml declares a permissions: key (zero hits), so the token scope depends on the repository default setting rather than the workflow; ci.yml likewise hands the token to coverallsapp/github-action@v2 (line 190) and Slack and Cypress steps.
- .github/workflows/image_actions.yml:35

Trust boundary crossings:
- tb-2 external → ci-cd-pipeline (internet-facing): Unscoped GITHUB_TOKEN weakens the token-scope assumption of the source-to-CI boundary, letting a compromised step write to the repository.

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-060 (F-060)
threats.mitigation:
M-134 — Drop unnecessary privileges in build and runtime (priority P3, effort Low)
1. Add top-level 'permissions: contents: read' to ci.yml and image_actions.yml, and grant 'contents: write' and 'pull-requests: write' only on the image_actions build job that creates the PR.
2. Set the repository default workflow permissions to read-only and add a workflow lint (zizmor or actionlint rule) that fails when a workflow lacks a permissions key.
Verification: grep -c '^permissions:' .github/workflows/ci.yml .github/workflows/image_actions.yml prints 1 for each file, and a test run shows the token cannot push to master from the coverage-report job.
Reference: https://docs.github.com/en/actions/security-for-github-actions/security-guides/automatic-token-authentication#modifying-the-permissions-for-the-github_token

threats.title: [F-061] Container Runs as Root — Dockerfile:1
threats.description:
Container Runs as Root: Containers running as root expand container-escape blast radius.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Medium, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-250
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: config-scan

Evidence:
- test/smoke/Dockerfile:1

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-061 (F-061)
threats.mitigation:
M-067 — Add non-root USER directive to test/smoke/Dockerfile (priority P3, effort Low)
1. In test/smoke/Dockerfile, after the FROM line add `RUN addgroup -S appgroup && adduser -S appuser -G appgroup` to create a dedicated non-root user, then add `USER appuser` as the final instruction before any CMD or ENTRYPOINT.
2. Run the smoke test job locally or in CI to confirm the container still executes its health-check commands successfully under the non-root user, and verify with `docker run --rm <image> id` that the output shows a uid other than 0.
Verification: grep -n '^USER' test/smoke/Dockerfile returns a line with a non-root username; docker run --rm <smoke-image> id outputs uid!=0; the smoke CI job exits 0.

threats.title: [F-062] Missing Workflow Permissions Block
threats.description:
Missing Workflow Permissions Block: Without an explicit permissions block at workflow or job level, the job inherits the repository default (commonly write-all) for GITHUB_TOKEN — any compromised step can push code, create releases, or approve PRs.

Risk: Medium (likelihood Medium, impact Medium)
CWE: CWE-732
Evidence tier: confirmed-exploitable
Source: config-scan

Evidence:
- .github/workflows/ci.yml:25

Full finding: threat-model.md#f-062 (F-062)
threats.mitigation:
M-068 — Add least-privilege permissions block to ci.yml (priority P3, effort Low)
1. Add `permissions: contents: read` at the top level of .github/workflows/ci.yml (immediately after the `on:` block), then grant elevated permissions only on the specific jobs that require them: `contents: write` for release and docker-push jobs, `packages: write` for Docker registry jobs, and `pull-requests: write` for any PR-creating jobs.
2. Set the repository default workflow token permissions to read-only under Settings > Actions > General, and add actionlint (or zizmor) as a CI step that fails the build when any workflow file under .github/workflows/ lacks a top-level or per-job permissions declaration.
Verification: grep -c '^permissions:' .github/workflows/ci.yml prints 1; actionlint exits 0 on the updated file; the full CI pipeline run confirms each job completes its required operations (docker push, npm publish, release creation) without permission errors.
